product spaces, let

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

$$T_kv:=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j.$$

Then $\operatorname{rank}T_k\le k$, one has

$$\lVert T-T_k\rVert=s_{k+1}$$

with the convention $s_{k+1}=0$ when $k\ge r$, and every linear map

$$\lVert T-A\rVert\ge s_{k+1}.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

singular value.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root.    $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$

   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$. Its **row space** $\operatorname{Row}(A)\subseteq F^n$ is the span of its rows, its **column space** $\operatorname{Col}(A)\subseteq F^m$ is the span of its columns, and its **nullspace** is
$$N(A):=\{x\in F^n:Ax=0\}.$$

The **row rank** and **column rank** are
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Row}(A),\qquad \operatorname{crank}(A):=\dim_F\operatorname{Col}(A).$$
These dimensions are defined because each space is spanned by a finite list.
Starting with the empty list, inspect the spanning vectors in order and retain a
vector exactly when it is not in the span of those already retained. Induction
shows that the retained list is independent and has the same span as the
original finite list, so it is a finite basis. The **rank** of $A$ is its row
rank; [[thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank]] proves that it also equals the column
rank.

For every finite matrix over a field,
$$\operatorname{rrank}(A)=\operatorname{crank}(A).$$
Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ and let $1\le r\le\min\{m,n\}$. Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.

   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two

   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, and let $f_x\in\mathbb R^p$ be the feature vector for each $x\in\mathcal X$. An approximate design $\xi$ and information matrix $M(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$ use the convention of [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. The same vectors may be scalar-observation sensitivities at a fixed parameter, as in [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], with a scalar precision absorbed into $f_x$. The procedure uses exact arithmetic.

**Input:** A finite nonempty $\mathcal X$, $p\ge1$, its feature vectors $(f_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, an approximate initial design $\xi^{(0)}$, and a finite nonnegative integer budget $N$ counting weight updates.

**Procedure:** Form $M_0=M(\xi^{(0)})$. If $M_0$ is not positive definite, return $(\xi^{(0)},\text{undefined violation},\text{invalid initial design})$. Otherwise, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, with current $\xi^{(k)}$ and $M_k=M(\xi^{(k)})$, compute
$$s_x^{(k)}=f_x^TM_k^{-1}f_x\quad(x\in\mathcal X),\qquad v_k=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}s_x^{(k)}-p.$$
If $v_k=0$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{equivalence-certified})$. If $k=N$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise set
$$\xi_x^{(k+1)}=\xi_x^{(k)}\frac{s_x^{(k)}}p\quad(x\in\mathcal X),$$
form $M_{k+1}=\sum_x\xi_x^{(k+1)}f_xf_x^T$, and continue.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

For the finite nonlinear observation design of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], fix $\theta\in\Theta$ and an approximate design $\xi$. The matrix $M_\theta(\xi)$ is positive definite, meaning symmetric with $v^TM_\theta(\xi)v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$, if and only if the stacked support sensitivity Jacobian $J_\xi(\theta)$ has trivial kernel, equivalently full column rank.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, let $p\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be the declared regression-vector map. Work under the stated linear mean model $Y=f(x)^{\mathsf T}\beta+\epsilon$, with mean-zero independent run errors of common variance $\sigma^2>0$. These are modeling assumptions, not claims about an experiment's empirical adequacy.

An **approximate design** is a weight function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x:\xi_x>0\}$ and its information matrix is
$$M(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}.$$
This matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A design is **nonsingular** when $M(\xi)$ is positive definite. For a singular design, the page's estimability convention is that a specified coefficient contrast $c^{\mathsf T}\beta$ is estimable exactly when $c\in\operatorname{span}\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\}$; the inverse-matrix criteria below are defined only for nonsingular designs.

For nonsingular designs on this fixed $f$ and $\mathcal X$, **D-optimality** maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$, **A-optimality** minimizes $\operatorname{tr}(M(\xi)^{-1})$, **E-optimality** maximizes $\lambda_{\min}(M(\xi))$, and **$c$-optimality** for a fixed $c\in\mathbb R^p$ minimizes $c^{\mathsf T}M(\xi)^{-1}c$; $c=0$ gives a trivial tie. The smallest eigenvalue is real because $M(\xi)$ is real symmetric ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]). These are different model- and candidate-dependent objectives; none is a universal design ranking.

An **exact $n$-run design**, for an integer $n\ge1$, has weights $\xi_x=n_x/n$ with nonnegative integer counts $n_x$ summing to $n$; optimizing over those integer allocations is a separate finite problem.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: Fix an update at a current approximate design with positive-definite $M=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$. For each $x$, put $s_x=f_x^TM^{-1}f_x$. Since $M$ is symmetric positive definite, $s_x\ge0$, and $s_x>0$ whenever $f_x\ne0$: writing $u=M^{-1}f_x$, one has $f_x^TM^{-1}f_x=u^TMu>0$ for $f_x\ne0$. By [F4] and [F5], $\sum_x\xi_xs_x=\sum_x\xi_x\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}f_xf_x^T)=\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}M)=\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$. Therefore $\xi_x^+=\xi_xs_x/p$ is nonnegative and $\sum_x\xi_x^+=1$, so it is again an approximate design.

For every feature $f_x$, a positive old weight remains positive after the update exactly when $f_x\ne0$: step 1.1 gives $s_x>0$ for nonzero $f_x$, and $s_x=0$ for $f_x=0$; zero weights remain zero. Thus the stacked scalar sensitivity matrix loses at most zero rows, so its kernel is unchanged. The current matrix is positive definite, so [F2] gives this kernel is trivial; applying [F2] to the new weights gives positive definiteness of the updated matrix. Induction applies this argument at every update, so no later inverse is undefined.

The loop checks one finite candidate set at each index $k=0,\ldots,N$, returns immediately on zero violation, and otherwise makes an update only when $k<N$. Thus it makes at most $N$ updates and at most $N+1$ sensitivity scans, and at $k=N$ returns the current design and its finite violation. The invariant argument above ensures every scan and update is well-defined.

An approximate design $\xi$ and information matrix $M(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$ use the convention of [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. The same vectors may be scalar-observation sensitivities at a fixed parameter, as in [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], with a scalar precision absorbed into $f_x$. The procedure uses exact arithmetic.

**Input:** A finite nonempty $\mathcal X$, $p\ge1$, its feature vectors $(f_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, an approximate initial design $\xi^{(0)}$, and a finite nonnegative integer budget $N$ counting weight updates.

**Procedure:** Form $M_0=M(\xi^{(0)})$. If $M_0$ is not positive definite, return $(\xi^{(0)},\text{undefined violation},\text{invalid initial design})$. Otherwise, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, with current $\xi^{(k)}$ and $M_k=M(\xi^{(k)})$, compute
$$s_x^{(k)}=f_x^TM_k^{-1}f_x\quad(x\in\mathcal X),\qquad v_k=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}s_x^{(k)}-p.$$
If $v_k=0$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{equivalence-certified})$. If $k=N$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise set
$$\xi_x^{(k+1)}=\xi_x^{(k)}\frac{s_x^{(k)}}p\quad(x\in\mathcal X),$$
form $M_{k+1}=\sum_x\xi_x^{(k+1)}f_xf_x^T$, and continue.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, let $p\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be the declared regression-vector map. Work under the stated linear mean model $Y=f(x)^{\mathsf T}\beta+\epsilon$, with mean-zero independent run errors of common variance $\sigma^2>0$. These are modeling assumptions, not claims about an experiment's empirical adequacy.

An **approximate design** is a weight function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x:\xi_x>0\}$ and its information matrix is
$$M(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}.$$
This matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A design is **nonsingular** when $M(\xi)$ is positive definite. For a singular design, the page's estimability convention is that a specified coefficient contrast $c^{\mathsf T}\beta$ is estimable exactly when $c\in\operatorname{span}\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\}$; the inverse-matrix criteria below are defined only for nonsingular designs.

For nonsingular designs on this fixed $f$ and $\mathcal X$, **D-optimality** maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$, **A-optimality** minimizes $\operatorname{tr}(M(\xi)^{-1})$, **E-optimality** maximizes $\lambda_{\min}(M(\xi))$, and **$c$-optimality** for a fixed $c\in\mathbb R^p$ minimizes $c^{\mathsf T}M(\xi)^{-1}c$; $c=0$ gives a trivial tie. The smallest eigenvalue is real because $M(\xi)$ is real symmetric ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]). These are different model- and candidate-dependent objectives; none is a universal design ranking.

An **exact $n$-run design**, for an integer $n\ge1$, has weights $\xi_x=n_x/n$ with nonnegative integer counts $n_x$ summing to $n$; optimizing over those integer allocations is a separate finite problem.

For $p\ge1$, if $A_0,A_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ are symmetric and $v^{\mathsf T}A_i v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and $i\in\{0,1\}$, then for every $t\in[0,1]$,
$$\log\det((1-t)A_0+tA_1)\ge(1-t)\log\det A_0+t\log\det A_1.$$

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $H$ be a direction matrix. Then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)H).$$

If $A$ is invertible, then

$$D\det(A)[H]=\det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}H).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$, and let $\xi^*$ be a nonsingular approximate design as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Whenever this holds, $u^*(x)=p$ for every $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi^*)$. No existence of a nonsingular optimum is asserted.

$$\sum_x\xi_xs_x=\sum_x\xi_x\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}f_xf_x^T)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(M^{-1}\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T\right)=\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}M)=\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p.$$
The first rank-one trace identity follows by expanding the diagonal sum: $\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}f_xf_x^T)=\sum_{i,j}(M^{-1})_{ij}(f_x)_j(f_x)_i=f_x^TM^{-1}f_x$. Since the $\xi_x$ are nonnegative and sum to one, their weighted average of the $s_x$ is at most their maximum. The displayed equality therefore gives $\max_xs_x\ge p$ and $v\ge0$.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

For a fixed design $\xi$, the observation map is **locally identifiable at $\theta_0\in\Theta$** if it is injective on some open neighborhood of $\theta_0$ in $\Theta$. It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open, and let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set of experimental conditions. For each $x\in\mathcal X$, let $q_x\ge1$, let $F_x:\Theta\to\mathbb R^{q_x}$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]], and let $W_x\in\mathbb R^{q_x\times q_x}$ be a symmetric positive-definite weight matrix, meaning $z^T W_x z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{q_x}$.

An **approximate design** is a function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$, as in [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x\in\mathcal X:\xi_x>0\}$. Define the joint observation map by
$$F_\xi(\theta)=(F_x(\theta))_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)},$$
where the finite product is ordered by any fixed listing of $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. Its **stacked sensitivity Jacobian** at $\theta$ is the vertical concatenation $J_\xi(\theta)$ of the matrices $J_x(\theta)=DF_x(\theta)$ for $x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)$. The associated **weighted information matrix** is
$$M_\theta(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x J_x(\theta)^T W_x J_x(\theta).$$
The matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite because each summand has nonnegative quadratic form.

Because the support is finite, $F_\xi$ is $C^1$ with derivative $J_\xi(\theta)$: the finite collection of component first-order remainders has a stacked Euclidean norm that is still $o(\|h\|_2)$, and the stacked derivative is continuous because each $DF_x$ is continuous.

It is **globally identifiable on $\Theta$** if it is injective on all of $\Theta$. A matrix $J:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m$ has full column rank when $Jv=0$ implies $v=0$. Its smallest singular value is $\sigma_{\min}(J)=\inf_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Jv\|_2$; thus $\sigma_{\min}(J)\ge\mu$ means $\|Jv\|_2\ge\mu\|v\|_2$ for every $v$.
where $M_h(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xJ_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}$.

Let $J,J_h\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, let $r=\min\{m,n\}$, and let $\sigma_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r(A)\ge0$ denote the singular values of a real matrix $A$. Then for every $1\le i\le r$,
$$|\sigma_i(J_h)-\sigma_i(J)|\le\|J_h-J\|_2,$$

Use the finite observation designs of [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]]. Suppose uniformly over $x\in\mathcal X$ that $\|J_x\|_2\le K$, $\|J_{h,x}-J_x\|_2\le\eta$, and $\|W_x\|_2\le w$, where $K,\eta,w\ge0$. For every approximate design $\xi$,
$$\|M_h(\xi)-M(\xi)\|_2\le\delta:=w(2K\eta+\eta^2),$$
where $M_h(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xJ_{h,x}^TW_xJ_{h,x}$. If $M(\xi)$ satisfies $v^TM(\xi)v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v$ with some $\alpha>\delta$, then
$$v^TM_h(\xi)v\ge(\alpha-\delta)\|v\|_2^2$$
for every $v$, so the computed information matrix remains positive definite.

Let $p\ge1$ and let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric. Put $E=B-A$ and $A_t=(1-t)A+tB$ for $0\le t\le1$. Suppose there is $\alpha>0$ such that $v^T A_t v\ge\alpha\|v\|_2^2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^p$ and every $t\in[0,1]$. Then $A_t$ is positive definite and

Suppose uniformly over $x\in\mathcal X$ that $\|J_x\|_2\le K$, $\|J_{h,x}-J_x\|_2\le\eta$, and $\|W_x\|_2\le w$, where $K,\eta,w\ge0$. Put $\delta=w(2K\eta+\eta^2)$. Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, let $p\ge1$, and let $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be the declared regression-vector map. Work under the stated linear mean model $Y=f(x)^{\mathsf T}\beta+\epsilon$, with mean-zero independent run errors of common variance $\sigma^2>0$. These are modeling assumptions, not claims about an experiment's empirical adequacy.

An **approximate design** is a weight function $\xi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x=1$. Its support is $\operatorname{supp}(\xi)=\{x:\xi_x>0\}$ and its information matrix is
$$M(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\xi_x f(x)f(x)^{\mathsf T}.$$
This matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite. A design is **nonsingular** when $M(\xi)$ is positive definite. For a singular design, the page's estimability convention is that a specified coefficient contrast $c^{\mathsf T}\beta$ is estimable exactly when $c\in\operatorname{span}\{f(x):x\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\}$; the inverse-matrix criteria below are defined only for nonsingular designs.

For nonsingular designs on this fixed $f$ and $\mathcal X$, **D-optimality** maximizes $\log\det M(\xi)$, **A-optimality** minimizes $\operatorname{tr}(M(\xi)^{-1})$, **E-optimality** maximizes $\lambda_{\min}(M(\xi))$, and **$c$-optimality** for a fixed $c\in\mathbb R^p$ minimizes $c^{\mathsf T}M(\xi)^{-1}c$; $c=0$ gives a trivial tie. The smallest eigenvalue is real because $M(\xi)$ is real symmetric ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]). These are different model- and candidate-dependent objectives; none is a universal design ranking.

An **exact $n$-run design**, for an integer $n\ge1$, has weights $\xi_x=n_x/n$ with nonnegative integer counts $n_x$ summing to $n$; optimizing over those integer allocations is a separate finite problem.

Let $p\ge1$, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, and let $f_x\in\mathbb R^p$ be the feature vector for each $x\in\mathcal X$. An approximate design $\xi$ and information matrix $M(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xf_xf_x^T$ use the convention of [[def-approximate-linear-model-design-and-optimality-criteria]]. The same vectors may be scalar-observation sensitivities at a fixed parameter, as in [[def-nonlinear-experimental-design-and-local-identifiability]], with a scalar precision absorbed into $f_x$. The procedure uses exact arithmetic.

**Input:** A finite nonempty $\mathcal X$, $p\ge1$, its feature vectors $(f_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, an approximate initial design $\xi^{(0)}$, and a finite nonnegative integer budget $N$ counting weight updates.

**Procedure:** Form $M_0=M(\xi^{(0)})$. If $M_0$ is not positive definite, return $(\xi^{(0)},\text{undefined violation},\text{invalid initial design})$. Otherwise, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, with current $\xi^{(k)}$ and $M_k=M(\xi^{(k)})$, compute
$$s_x^{(k)}=f_x^TM_k^{-1}f_x\quad(x\in\mathcal X),\qquad v_k=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}s_x^{(k)}-p.$$
If $v_k=0$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{equivalence-certified})$. If $k=N$, return $(\xi^{(k)},v_k,\text{budget-exhausted})$. Otherwise set
$$\xi_x^{(k+1)}=\xi_x^{(k)}\frac{s_x^{(k)}}p\quad(x\in\mathcal X),$$
form $M_{k+1}=\sum_x\xi_x^{(k+1)}f_xf_x^T$, and continue.

For the algorithm [[alg-finite-budget-multiplicative-d-optimal-design]], suppose the initial weights form an approximate design and its information matrix is positive definite. Then every update preserves nonnegative weights summing to one and positive definiteness of the information matrix. For every finite budget $N$, the procedure returns after at most $N$ updates and at most $N+1$ sensitivity scans.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty candidate set, let $p\ge1$, and let $\xi$ be any returned nonsingular approximate design from [[alg-finite-budget-multiplicative-d-optimal-design]]. Put $M=M(\xi)$ and
$$s_x=f_x^TM^{-1}f_x,\qquad v=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}s_x-p.$$
Then $v\ge0$, every nonsingular approximate competitor $\eta$ satisfies
$$\log\det M(\eta)-\log\det M(\xi)\le v,$$
and $v=0$ if and only if $\xi$ is D-optimal among nonsingular approximate designs.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For an arbitrary approximate design $\xi$, write $\mu=\sum_t\xi_tt$ and $
u=\sum_t\xi_tt^2$. Direct multiplication gives $M(\xi)= egin{bmatrix}1&\mu\\mu&
u\end{bmatrix}$ and $\det M(\xi)=
u-\mu^2$. Since $0\le t\le2$, $(t-1)^2\le1$, so $
u-\mu^2=\sum_t\xi_t(t-1)^2-(\mu-1)^2\le1$. The equal endpoint design $\xi^*=(1/2,0,1/2)$ has $M(\xi^*)= egin{bmatrix}1&1\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ and determinant $1$, so it maximizes the determinant and hence $\log\det M$ among nonsingular designs because $\log$ is strictly increasing by [F5].

For $\xi^{(0)}$, $M_0=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&5/3\end{bmatrix}$ and $M_0^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}5/2&-3/2\\-3/2&3/2\end{bmatrix}$. Thus $(s_0,s_1,s_2)=(5/2,1,5/2)$ and $v_0=1/2$. One update gives $\xi^{(1)}=(5/12,1/6,5/12)$; the update is defined by [F2] and remains nonsingular by [F3].

The updated matrix is $M_1=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&11/6\end{bmatrix}$, with inverse $M_1^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}11/5&-6/5\\-6/5&6/5\end{bmatrix}$. Therefore $(s_0,s_1,s_2)=(11/5,1,11/5)$ and $v_1=11/5-2=1/5$. With budget $N=1$, the procedure returns the updated design with status budget-exhausted and violation $1/5$.

For the endpoint design $\xi^*$, $M(\xi^*)^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$, so its sensitivities at $0,1,2$ are $2,1,2$ and its violation is zero. By [F4] this is an exact D-optimality certificate; [F4] also bounds the log-determinant gap of the one-update output by $1/5$. The weights are approximate-design weights; integer run counts are a separate problem by [F1].
